nodes.name: Deltoid
nodes.location: Caps the shoulder at the front, outer side and back, from the collarbone and the shoulder blade down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Its front part raises your arm forward and turns it inward, its outer part raises the arm out to the side, and its back part moves the arm backward and turns it outward. It also helps hold the shoulder steady.
nodes.shapeNote: Together its three parts make up most of the rounded outline of the shoulder. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for its three parts.
The three parts are a teaching simplification: anatomy studies divide the deltoid into more segments, five to eight in one study of its nerve branches, and the count differs between people.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Superficial over the whole shoulder; references call it easily observed and palpated and say it gives the shoulder its rounded contour (kenhub.deltoid, elsevier.deltoid, statpearls.deltoid).
nodes.layerCheck: Parent node, not drawn (layer '—' in §1.2). All three parts are surface muscles, so 'surface' is the honest value if the type needs one.

nodes.name: Anterior deltoid
nodes.location: Front of the shoulder, from the outer third of the collarbone down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Raises your arm forward and turns it inward. It also helps bring a raised arm across the front of the chest and helps raise the arm out to the side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the front of the rounded shoulder outline, beside the upper chest, where a groove separates it from the pectoralis major. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Presses and front raises load it together with the upper chest; how the work splits between them changes with the exercise and the bench angle.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin at the front of the shoulder and bounded from the chest by the deltopectoral groove (kenhub.deltoid, radiopaedia.deltopectoral_groove).

nodes.name: Lateral deltoid
nodes.location: Outer side of the shoulder, from the outer edge of the bony tip of the shoulder (the acromion) down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Raises your arm out to the side. It does most of the lifting once the movement has started; the supraspinatus helps start it.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the outer curve of the shoulder. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Studies call this part the middle, lateral or medial deltoid; all three names mean the same part.
Raising the arm out to the side also works the supraspinatus, which lies under the trapezius and the bony tip of the shoulder.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin on the outer side of the shoulder (kenhub.deltoid, elsevier.deltoid_acromial).

nodes.name: Posterior deltoid
nodes.location: Back of the shoulder, from the bony ridge of the shoulder blade (its spine) down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Moves a raised arm backward, brings the arm back and down from in front of the body, and turns the arm outward.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the back of the rounded shoulder outline, over parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: In one comparison it worked harder in a reverse fly than in a seated row or a pulldown.
Turning the arm outward loads it together with the infraspinatus and teres minor.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin at the back of the shoulder; it covers parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor rather than being covered (kenhub.deltoid, kenhub.infraspinatus, kenhub.teres_minor).

nodes.name: Rotator cuff
nodes.location: Four muscles from the shoulder blade to the top of the upper-arm bone, wrapping the shoulder joint at the front, the top and the back.
nodes.whatItDoes: Holds the ball of the upper-arm bone in its shallow socket while the arm moves, and turns the arm inward and outward.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly deep, under the deltoid and the trapezius, so as a group it has little or no contour of its own; only parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor reach the surface, on the back of the shoulder blade. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the four muscles inside it.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Supraspinatus and subscapularis are covered; parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor are not covered by other muscles (kenhub.infraspinatus, kenhub.teres_minor).
nodes.layerCheck: Parent node, not drawn (layer '—' in §1.2). All four members are 'deep' in §1.2, so 'deep' is the honest value if the type needs one.

nodes.name: Supraspinatus
nodes.location: Top of the shoulder blade, above its bony ridge and under the trapezius; its tendon runs under the bony tip of the shoulder to the top of the upper-arm bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Helps raise your arm out to the side, working with the deltoid; anatomy texts describe it as starting the movement. It also helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies under the trapezius and the bony tip of the shoulder, so it has little or no visible contour of its own.
caveats: Raising the arm to the side works it together with the deltoid; testing studies found positions that favour it, not ones that isolate it.
Anatomy texts stress its role at the start of the movement; it also aids the deltoid after that, and the deltoid does most of the lifting.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Covered by the trapezius, with its tendon under the acromion (kenhub.supraspinatus, statpearls.supraspinatus).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep: supported (under the trapezius; kenhub.supraspinatus). No outcrop claimed, none found.

nodes.name: Infraspinatus
nodes.location: Back of the shoulder blade, below its bony ridge; its tendon crosses the back of the shoulder joint to the top of the upper-arm bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your arm outward, and helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Covers most of the back of the shoulder blade below its ridge. Much of it lies under the trapezius, the back of the deltoid and the latissimus dorsi, so it has little separately visible contour of its own; where it is not covered it may contribute to the contour on the back of the shoulder blade. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Turning the arm outward works it together with the teres minor and the back of the deltoid; how the work splits between them changes with arm position and is not known exactly.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Kenhub places it deep to the trapezius and only parts of the deltoid and latissimus dorsi, which leaves part of it uncovered on the back of the shoulder blade (kenhub.infraspinatus).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep with a back-view surface outcrop: supported by kenhub.infraspinatus ('deep to trapezius, and parts of the deltoid and latissimus dorsi'). elsevier.infraspinatus says deep to the trapezius and deltoid without saying 'parts of'; not a contradiction of the outcrop, but less specific.

nodes.name: Teres minor
nodes.location: Outer edge of the shoulder blade on the back, just below the infraspinatus and above the teres major; its tendon reaches the top of the upper-arm bone from behind.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your arm outward, alongside the infraspinatus, and helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Narrow, and partly covered by the back of the deltoid, so it has little separately visible contour of its own; at the outer edge of the shoulder blade it is hard to tell apart from the infraspinatus and the teres major. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It turns the arm outward together with the infraspinatus, so outward-turning work loads both.
Not the teres major, the muscle just below it, which belongs to the back.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Kenhub says the deltoid covers its upper outer part, leaving the rest near the surface; it is narrow and lies between the infraspinatus and teres major (kenhub.teres_minor, statpearls.teres_minor).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep with a back-view surface outcrop: supported by kenhub.teres_minor (the deltoid covers its superolateral aspect). statpearls.teres_minor calls it 'located deep to the deltoid' without qualification; the two read differently, and the outcrop rests on Kenhub. §7.2 already allows it to be list-only if it cannot hold a 44 px square.

nodes.name: Subscapularis
nodes.location: Front, rib-facing surface of the shoulder blade; its tendon crosses the front of the shoulder joint to the upper-arm bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your arm inward, and helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket. It is the largest muscle of the rotator cuff.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies on the rib-facing side of the shoulder blade, under other structures, so it has little or no visible contour of its own.
caveats: Its upper and lower parts can be recorded separately, and in studies arm position changed which part worked harder.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: On the costal surface of the scapula, behind the serratus anterior and the shoulder joint (elsevier.subscapularis, kenhub.subscapularis).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep: supported. Drawing note (not a §1.2 change): from the front only its tendon and outer part cross in front of the joint (statpearls.subscapularis); the belly lies behind the rib cage in a front view.

sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: the prime flexors of the glenohumeral joint are the deltoid (anterior fibres) and pectoralis major (clavicular fibres). No passage on horizontal adduction or abduction was returned from this page.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: deltoid muscle (left)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: the thick triangular muscle that gives the shoulder its rounded contour; superficial to the glenohumeral joint, the proximal tendons of biceps brachii and triceps brachii, and the axillary nerve; flexes and medially rotates the arm when the clavicular part contracts on its own.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: clavicular part of deltoid muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: from the lateral third of the clavicle to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus; its main actions at the glenohumeral joint are flexion and medial rotation of the arm; it helps with transverse adduction of the flexed arm and helps stabilise the shoulder joint.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: acromial part of deltoid muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: arises from the lateral aspect of the acromion; the acromial, clavicular and scapular spinal parts converge on a short, thick tendon to the deltoid tuberosity; it is the abductor of the arm at the shoulder joint, and simultaneous contraction of supraspinatus is needed to initiate abduction from the anatomical position; axillary nerve (C5-C6).

sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: from the spine of the scapula to the deltoid tuberosity; 'Extends, laterally rotates and transversely abducts arm at glenohumeral (shoulder) joint'; axillary nerve (C5-C6). sources.title: Hik and Ackland, The moment arms of the muscles spanning the glenohumeral joint: a systematic review (Journal of Anatomy 234(1):1-15)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): pooled moment arms of the deltoid, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major and the four rotator cuff muscles during abduction, flexion and axial rotation; the anterior and middle deltoid sub-regions had the largest humeral elevator moment arms of all muscles during coronal- and scapular-plane abduction and during flexion; the posterior deltoid and teres minor can act as abductors or adductors depending on arm position; infraspinatus and teres minor oppose subscapularis in a transverse-plane force couple that compresses the humeral head into the glenoid. sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, also PMC3042752): in 60 cadaver shoulders the deltoid divided into seven segments by the distribution of its intramuscular tendons; FDG-PET uptake after scapular-plane elevation was uneven and matched the segments, which the authors took to be the muscle's functional units. sources.title: Audenaert and Barbaix, deltoid segments defined by axillary nerve branching (Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, British volume, supplement abstract)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (conference abstract): 44 deltoids from 22 embalmed adult cadavers divided by the axillary nerve branch supplying each portion: eight major divisions in 3, seven in 22 of 44, six in 14 and five in 5; the authors conclude that a segmentation into five to eight major segments is found, and cite mechanomyographic work describing at least seven functional segments in a muscle usually taught as three. Exact title and year not shown. A related paper by the same authors, 'Separate segments within the deltoid muscle: anatomical variants or wishful thinking?' (PMC2840820), was seen but its conclusions were not.

sources.title: Coratella et al., An Electromyographic Analysis of Lateral Raise Variations and Frontal Raise in Competitive Bodybuilders (International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(17):6015, 2020)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, two searches): ten competitive bodybuilders; surface EMG of the anterior, medial (lateral) and posterior deltoid, pectoralis major, upper trapezius and triceps brachii during lateral raises with the humerus externally rotated, neutral and internally rotated, a lateral raise with the elbow flexed, and a frontal raise. Concentric phase: anterior deltoid greater in the frontal raise than in all others; medial deltoid greater in the neutral lateral raise than in the externally rotated, frontal and flexed-elbow versions; posterior deltoid greater in the internally rotated lateral raise than in all others; similar patterns in the eccentric phase. The abstract's conclusion also says humeral external rotation increases anterior and medial deltoid activation, which reads against the medial result unless it compares with internal rotation; the claims rely only on the results lines. The PubMed id is read from an index record (OLB-PM-32824894), not from PubMed itself; the DOI was not shown. Acute activity, not growth.

sources.title: Campos, Vianna, Guimaraes, Oliveira, Hernandez-Mosqueira, da Silva and Marchetti, Different Shoulder Exercises Affect the Activation of Deltoid Portions in Resistance-Trained Individuals (Journal of Human Kinetics 75:5-14, 2020)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract and library records, bibliorepositorio.unach.cl): 13 resistance-trained men; one set of 12 repetitions at 60 percent of one-repetition maximum per exercise; surface EMG normalised to maximal isometric contractions. Anterior deltoid highest in the shoulder press (bench press, lateral raise and dumbbell fly did not differ from one another); medial deltoid higher in the lateral raise and shoulder press than in the bench press and dumbbell fly; posterior deltoid highest in the lateral raise, and higher in the shoulder press than in the bench press and fly. DOI and PubMed id not shown. Acute activity, not growth.

sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract and conclusion, also PMC7579505): 30 trained adults at 60 percent of one-repetition maximum on benches at 0, 15, 30, 45 and 60 degrees; anterior deltoid EMG highest at 60 degrees; inclinations greater than 45 degrees produce significantly higher anterior deltoid activation and decrease the muscular performance of the pectoralis major; triceps similar at all angles. sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Rotator Cuff
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026: subscapularis, infraspinatus, teres minor and supraspinatus ('SITS') arise from the scapula and insert on the humerus; compression is the core function, pressing the humeral head into the glenoid, and the cuff contracts during arm movements to keep the head from sliding; the tendons blend with the capsule at the back, top and front of the joint, leaving the bottom open; static and dynamic stabilisers (the cuff and the long head of biceps); supraspinatus primarily starts abduction and subscapularis medially rotates, with infraspinatus and teres minor listed for lateral rotation (that line was not captured verbatim). Versions dated 2023 and 2026 appeared.

disagreements: Starting abduction. StatPearls (deltoid) says the deltoid cannot start abduction and Elsevier (acromial part) says the supraspinatus is needed to start it; Kenhub says the supraspinatus is essential for the early range. No source seen tested whether the supraspinatus matters beyond the start. Wording: the supraspinatus 'helps raise the arm' and references 'describe it as starting the movement'; its caveat says references differ on its role beyond the start.

Teres minor cover. StatPearls: 'located deep to the deltoid'; Kenhub: the deltoid covers its superolateral aspect. The appearance claim says the deltoid covers its upper outer part (Kenhub) and the outcrop in §1.2 rests on Kenhub.

Infraspinatus as a rotator. A 2024 case report's introduction (PMC11013571, 'Novel Muscle in Infraspinous Fossa') says it makes only a minor contribution to lateral rotation and mainly stabilises; StatPearls, Elsevier and Kenhub list external rotation as its action. Not cited; the claim keeps the reference texts' action and also states the stabilising role.

Coratella 2020. The results lines say the medial deltoid was more active in the neutral lateral raise than the externally rotated one; the conclusion line says external rotation increases anterior and medial deltoid activation (probably against internal rotation). The lateral-deltoid selectivity claim uses only the results lines.

Rodriguez-Ridao 2020. The abstract's overall conclusion says the flat bench gives similar pectoralis and anterior deltoid activity, while the conclusion quoted from the full text says inclines above 45 degrees raise anterior deltoid activity. The claim states the incline finding and the authors' conclusion only.

Anterior deltoid at low abduction angles. Physiopedia says the clavicular and spinal parts adduct below about 60 degrees and abduct above it; the moment-arm studies rank the anterior part among the most effective abductors. The anterior deltoid's abduction row is 'assist', and no abduction row is given to the posterior part.

Subscapularis tests. Tokish 2003 found the belly-press and lift-off tests favoured different parts; a later study (Pennock 2011, not cited) found three tests did not differ. The claim reports Tokish as one study.

A generated summary (Q25) said the posterior deltoid's external rotation was found only on a flashcard site, while Elsevier, Loyola and Kenhub each list it. The specific references are cited; this is an example of the summaries' limits.
deliberatelyNotClaimed: Horizontal abduction for the infraspinatus and teres minor: Elsevier lists it ('transversely abducts') and nothing else seen does; left out of node actions, as the forearm left out minor actions.
Weak external rotation by the supraspinatus (StatPearls 'possible weak contribution'): left out.
Adduction by the teres minor and subscapularis: said in their function claims, but shoulder.adduction is not a shoulders region action (it belongs to the chest and back).
Horizontal abduction by the lateral deltoid (Physiopedia; Botton found more middle-deltoid activity in the reverse peck deck than the pulldown): not claimed.
Variation claims for the rotator cuff: infraspinatus and teres minor fusion and accessory subscapularis slips were found only as single-specimen case reports (Wikipedia read, not cited).
A teres minor selectivity claim: no study recording it on its own was seen with results (Reinold 2004's results were not shown; a physiotherapy blog's account was not used).
Trebs 2010 (incline bench): seen only secondhand; not cited.
IMAIOS deltoid: its lines were merged with other sites in the summary, so they were not attributed or cited.
No clinical content: tear rates and testing accuracy are not stated as claims; the testing studies are cited only for what they measured in healthy people.
